q: Which statement about UTI terminology is FALSE?
o: Bacteriuria plus pyuria always equals UTI, and urine is normally sterile
Bacteriuria without pyuria usually means colonisation
Acute pyelonephritis is a clinical syndrome of chills, fever and flank pain with bacteriuria and pyuria
Uncomplicated UTI occurs in healthy people with normal urinary tracts; complicated UTI involves factors that make bacteriuria more likely and treatment less effective
e: Bacteriuria and pyuria do not mean UTI on their own, and urine is not sterile: RNA sequencing shows a female urinary microbiome, now studied with expanded quantitative urine culture (EQUC). UTIs are classified by their likely site of origin. They are the commonest bacterial infection. Urine results can only be interpreted alongside the symptoms.
s: Ch 55 Urinary tract infections

q: Which statement about recurrent UTI is FALSE?
o: Antimicrobial treatment changes only the time to recurrence, not the overall risk
Most recurrences in women are reinfections, by ascent from bowel flora or re-emergence from intracellular bacterial colonies
Persistence (the same strain) recurs quickly; reinfection recurs later
Recurrent uncomplicated UTIs commonly cause renal scarring, hypertension and renal failure
e: No link has been shown between recurrent uncomplicated UTI and renal scarring, hypertension or progressive renal failure, so the long-term effect is minimal. Find and remove any source of persistence. Prevention should focus on non-antibiotic measures.
s: Ch 55 Urinary tract infections

q: Which factor does LEAST to promote ascending infection?
o: Intermittent or indwelling catheters
Spermicide use
Faecal soiling of the perineum
Frequent voiding
e: Voiding is the bladder's main defence, because whether a small inoculum survives depends on emptying. Obstruction is a key host factor. Most UTIs come from bowel flora.
s: Ch 55 Urinary tract infections

q: Which pairing of organism and setting is correct?
o: Nosocomial UTIs are caused mainly by sensitive bowel flora
Pseudomonas typically causes community cystitis
S. epidermidis is the commonest cause of cystitis in young women
S. saprophyticus causes about 10% of lower UTIs in young sexually active women and rarely infects men or the elderly
e: Healthcare-associated UTIs (hospital or institution) involve Pseudomonas and more resistant organisms. Catheterisation is the most common predisposing factor. Catheter-associated bacteriuria is the commonest hospital-acquired infection.
s: Ch 55 Urinary tract infections

q: Which statement about virulence and host susceptibility is FALSE?
o: Pili (FimH on type 1 pili binding urothelial receptors) are the key adherence factor
P-piliated E. coli rarely cause pyelonephritis in women without reflux
Increased bacterial adherence to vaginal cells was the first biological difference shown in UTI-prone women, and epithelial receptivity is a genotypic trait
Phase variation of pili affects virulence: type 1 pili help colonisation but also increase phagocytosis
e: Without reflux, P-piliated E. coli binding P blood-group antigens are the commonest cause of acute pyelonephritis in young women. Virulence factors such as adhesins determine which bacteria invade and how far.
s: Ch 55 Urinary tract infections

q: Which statement is FALSE?
o: Enterococcus, Pseudomonas and most Gram-positive bacteria do not produce nitrite
Many squamous cells suggest the midstream sample is contaminated
Vaginal atrophy, poor manual dexterity, inability to bear weight and a pessary all favour a catheter specimen
Dipstick testing is preferred over formal urinalysis
e: Formal urinalysis is preferred, and culture gives sensitivities. A history of HPV does not affect sample quality. In recurrent UTI, ask about spermicide use, childhood voiding dysfunction, previous urological surgery, and past organisms and antibiotics. A family history of postmenopausal UTI is the least relevant.
s: Ch 55 Urinary tract infections

q: Which imaging statement is correct?
o: Image at once if fever persists 24 hours on treatment
Image all women with recurrent UTI
Ultrasound is the most sensitive for renal abscess
Imaging and cystoscopy are NOT routinely needed in women with recurrent uncomplicated UTI; CT (or MRI) is the most sensitive for renal abscess, focal bacterial nephritis and radiolucent stones
e: Image men, children, spinal cord injury patients and women with complicated features. In uncomplicated pyelonephritis fever can last several days on correct antibiotics, so a fever at 24 hours alone needs only observation. Image if there is no response after about 72 hours.
s: Ch 55 Urinary tract infections

q: Which statement is FALSE?
o: Nitrofurantoin works because it is briefly concentrated in urine and does not alter bowel flora
Cure depends mainly on the urine antibiotic level and how long it stays above the MIC
Treatment success depends mainly on serum levels
Unresolved bacteriuria during treatment is most often due to initial resistance of the organism
e: Choose antibiotics on efficacy, safety, cost and adherence. Overuse drives resistance, so both the agent and the duration matter.
s: Ch 55 Urinary tract infections

q: For acute uncomplicated cystitis in women, which regimen fits IDSA 2010 guidance?
o: Nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days, or TMP-SMX DS twice daily for 3 days
TMP-SMX 7–14 days
Ciprofloxacin 14 days
Amoxicillin 3 days
e: Confirm sensitivity on culture if symptoms persist. Single-dose fosfomycin is another first-line option in current guidelines.
s: Ch 55 Urinary tract infections

q: Screening for and treating asymptomatic bacteriuria is indicated in:
o: Confused or incontinent patients
Catheterised or spinal cord injury patients
Pregnant women, and patients before urological procedures that breach the mucosa
The elderly
e: Treating it in other groups gives no benefit in symptoms or survival, and causes side effects, resistant reinfection and cost, including in nursing-home residents. Untreated asymptomatic bacteriuria does not cause hypertension or renal failure. Most elderly people with bacteriuria have no symptoms. Prevalence varies with age, sex and comorbidity, and rises with institutional care.
s: Ch 55 Urinary tract infections

q: Which statement about UTI in pregnancy is FALSE?
o: Ciprofloxacin is preferred for pyelonephritis
Screen all women with urine culture in the first trimester
The prevalence of bacteriuria is no higher than outside pregnancy, but it rarely clears spontaneously and more often progresses to pyelonephritis (20–40% if untreated)
Pyelonephritis in pregnancy is linked mainly to maternal sepsis
e: Fluoroquinolones may damage fetal cartilage. Trimethoprim is a folate antagonist, linked to neural tube and heart defects in the first trimester and megaloblastic anaemia. Nitrofurantoin does not reach blood levels, so it cannot treat pyelonephritis. Oral cephalexin is suitable. Penicillins and cephalosporins are safe throughout pregnancy, with nitrofurantoin an alternative for cystitis (avoid near term). Treat all bacteriuria in pregnancy.
s: Ch 55 Urinary tract infections

q: Which statement about vaginal oestrogen is correct?
o: It increases thrombosis
It only relieves vaginal pain
It works immediately
It reduces recurrent UTI by lowering vaginal pH and restoring lactobacilli; benefit may take at least 12 weeks; observational data show no increase in breast cancer or fractures
e: Randomised trials were not powered for cancer or cardiovascular outcomes.
s: Ch 55 Urinary tract infections

q: Which statement is FALSE?
o: Chronic pyelonephritis usually presents with flank pain and fever
Most patients with emphysematous pyelonephritis are managed with antibiotics, bladder drainage, glucose control or percutaneous drainage; surgery is for failures
A small perirenal abscess in a functioning kidney is treated by percutaneous drainage
Emphysematous pyelonephritis mainly affects diabetic women, and in diabetics can occur without obstruction
e: Chronic pyelonephritis is silent until renal failure develops. Renal abscesses are seen well on CT and treated with IV antibiotics plus drainage, while small ones may settle with antibiotics alone. Pyonephrosis (an infected hydronephrotic kidney) needs urgent IV antibiotics and drainage. Acute pyelonephritis shows wedge-shaped areas of poor enhancement on CT. It can range from cystitis-like symptoms to sepsis.
s: Ch 55 Urinary tract infections

q: The most important complication of renal papillary necrosis is:
o: Cancer
Abscess
Ureteric obstruction by a sloughed papilla, a urological emergency if infected
Renal failure
e: Infected obstruction needs urgent drainage.
s: Ch 55 Urinary tract infections

q: Which statement about xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis is FALSE?
o: It can mimic a renal tumour and inflame the retroperitoneum; nephrectomy is usually needed
The kidney is usually small and shrunken
Proteus is the commonest organism, with E. coli also common
It arises in a poorly functioning kidney obstructed by stones, with foamy macrophages
e: The kidney is usually enlarged, often with a staghorn stone. A small, scarred kidney with gas and fluid tracking into the flank suggests a perinephric abscess. Partial nephrectomy is possible only for focal disease in a functioning kidney.
s: Ch 55 Urinary tract infections

q: Malakoplakia is characterised by:
o: Von Hansemann histiocytes containing Michaelis–Gutmann bodies (calcified lysosomal inclusions), due to defective macrophage killing, usually of E. coli; treat with prolonged antibiotics that reach high levels inside cells
Being premalignant
Caseating granulomas
Treatment with BCG
e: It appears as soft yellow-brown plaques ('soft plaque'). Michaelis and Gutmann described it in 1902 and von Hansemann in 1903. Suitable antibiotics include sulfonamides, TMP-SMX and fluoroquinolones.
s: Ch 55 Urinary tract infections

q: Renal echinococcosis is managed by:
o: Aspiration alone
Antibiotics
Observation
Surgical removal of the intact cyst; if it ruptures or must be marsupialised, aspirate and instil a scolicidal agent first
e: Rupture causes seeding, anaphylaxis and recurrence. Perioperative albendazole is commonly added in current practice.
s: Ch 55 Urinary tract infections

q: The earliest reliable clinical sign of bacteraemia or sepsis is:
o: Hyperventilation (respiratory alkalosis)
Confusion
Fever
Chills
e: Sepsis means abnormal temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate or white cell count in response to infection. Management: resuscitation, support, monitoring, broad-spectrum antibiotics and source control. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign and early goal-directed therapy improve outcomes.
s: Ch 55 Urinary tract infections

q: Which statement is FALSE?
o: Asymptomatic catheter-associated bacteriuria should always be treated
In spinal cord injury, UTI presents as fever, flank or abdominal discomfort, leaking between catheterisations, more spasticity, lethargy, or cloudy smelly urine; culture before treatment
Bacteriuria causes the most severe illness in spinal cord injury patients
Clean intermittent catheterisation has the lowest long-term complication rate
e: Catheter bacteriuria is inevitable, so treat only symptomatic infection. Aseptic insertion with a closed, dependent drainage system is the most effective prevention. Transplant UTI risk factors include a cadaveric graft, diabetes, long pre-transplant dialysis, female sex and two episodes of asymptomatic bacteriuria. Polycystic native kidneys are not a risk factor.
s: Ch 55 Urinary tract infections

q: Which statement about Fournier gangrene is FALSE?
o: Urgent debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics is essential
It is necrotising fasciitis arising from the perineal skin, scrotum, urethra or rectum
Obesity is the classic key risk factor in the chapter
Risk factors include diabetes, urethral stricture with extravasation, instrumentation, paraphimosis, perirectal infection and local trauma or surgery
e: The chapter does not list obesity. A periurethral abscess (from stricture or catheterisation) is treated by debridement, suprapubic diversion and antibiotics.
s: Ch 55 Urinary tract infections

q: Which statement on surgical antibiotic prophylaxis is correct, according to the chapter?
o: Give within 60–120 minutes of the start and cover the procedure; the need depends on the procedure and the patient's host defences
Give endocarditis prophylaxis for all prosthetic valves in GU surgery
Give the evening before
Give routinely for all orthopaedic implants
e: AHA: no prophylaxis solely to prevent endocarditis for GU procedures, even in high-risk cardiac patients. The 2003 joint statement suggested prophylaxis only for high-risk joints, such as those implanted within 2 years. Current AUA guidance does not routinely recommend it for implants. Special groups: TRUS biopsy, bacteriuria, endocarditis risk, and orthopaedic hardware. AUA timing is usually within 60 minutes (120 minutes for fluoroquinolones and vancomycin).
s: Ch 55 Urinary tract infections (updated)

q: A patient improving on antibiotics for acute pyelonephritis still has an enlarged kidney, and a biopsy shows neutrophils in the interstitium and tubules. The biopsy:
o: Guides how long to treat
Means antibiotics should change
Was unnecessary; enlargement can persist for weeks with correct treatment
Predicts an abscess
e: Neutrophils in the tubules form white cell casts.
s: Ch 55 Urinary tract infections

q: Which pairing of NIH prostatitis category is correct?
o: Category II: acute febrile prostatitis
Category IIIA: CPPS with no inflammation
Category IIIB: pelvic pain, negative cultures, no white cells in EPS, VB3 or semen; category IV: asymptomatic inflammation found incidentally (no treatment needed)
Category IV: chronic pain with inflammation
e: I: acute bacterial. II: chronic bacterial. IIIA: CPPS with inflammation. IIIB: CPPS without inflammation. IV: asymptomatic inflammatory, found on biopsy for BPH, cancer or infertility. Do not give antibiotics to 'treat' a raised PSA with category IV inflammation. Follow PSA and DRE.
s: Ch 56 Prostatitis, orchitis, epididymitis and scrotal pain

q: Which statement about category I acute bacterial prostatitis is FALSE?
o: Use a urethral catheter for long-term drainage
E. coli is the commonest organism overall; Pseudomonas is much commoner after urinary tract manipulation
Organisms and sensitivities differ for spontaneous, post-transurethral and post-transrectal biopsy cases
Fever after transrectal biopsy: give carbapenem, amikacin or second/third-generation cephalosporin, not fluoroquinolone or TMP-SMX
e: Use a suprapubic tube if long-term drainage is needed. If there is no response, image to look for an abscess. Abscesses under 1–2 cm can be treated with antibiotics. Larger or non-responding ones need percutaneous aspiration or transurethral unroofing. It presents with acute dysuria and frequency, with or without fever.
s: Ch 56 Prostatitis, orchitis, epididymitis and scrotal pain

q: A 41-year-old has a second UTI in 4 months with the same E. coli. Which is correct?
o: Exclude retention with uroflow and post-void residual (cystoscopy if flow is poor, to find a stricture); men under 45 do not need upper-tract imaging
STI test is essential
CT urogram
Four-glass test is mandatory
e: Chronic bacterial prostatitis means recurrent UTI with the same organism, with few symptoms between episodes (unlike CPPS). Treat with antibiotics that penetrate the prostate. For refractory cases use daily suppression or TURP. Test for STIs only if there is urethral discharge.
s: Ch 56 Prostatitis, orchitis, epididymitis and scrotal pain

q: A man with autoimmune pancreatitis has a TURP for retention. Histology is likely to show:
o: IgG4-positive plasma cells with characteristic fibrosis
No inflammation
Granulomatous prostatitis
Heavy lymphocytic infiltrate in the ducts
e: IgG4-related disease also includes retroperitoneal fibrosis (Ormond disease) and responds dramatically to steroids.
s: Ch 56 Prostatitis, orchitis, epididymitis and scrotal pain

q: Which statement about CP/CPPS is FALSE?
o: Men with CPPS have the same bacterial counts in urine, prostatic fluid and semen as men without pain
There is evidence of central sensitisation, increased pain sensitivity, and a low baseline ACTH with a blunted stress response
Men with more white cells in EPS have worse symptoms
White cells in EPS do not correlate with symptoms
e: CP/CPPS is a diagnosis of exclusion. Problems often extend beyond the pelvis, such as psychological and neurological issues.
s: Ch 56 Prostatitis, orchitis, epididymitis and scrotal pain

q: Which statement about CPPS is correct?
o: Anger predicts pain
Stress predicted flares in MAPP
Fibromyalgia is the commonest overlap
Catastrophising and helplessness predict pain, urinary symptoms and depression; IBS is the commonest overlapping pain condition; men with CPPS have more premature ejaculation and ejaculatory pain
e: In the MAPP case-crossover study only recent sexual activity and UTI-like symptoms predicted flares. Diet, activity, stress and constipation did not. Assess for IBS, fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue. Cognitive behavioural therapy can help catastrophising.
s: Ch 56 Prostatitis, orchitis, epididymitis and scrotal pain

q: Which statement is FALSE?
o: Pseudodyssynergy is sphincter EMG activity during voiding, without straining, in a neurologically intact man, indicating pelvic floor dysfunction
The GUPI adds questions on bladder (filling) pain, present in about 40% of men in MAPP
Symptom assessment and pelvic floor examination are optional
Cystoscopy is optional: used for poor flow or raised residual (stricture), or bladder-related pain (to look for Hunner lesions)
e: Symptom assessment, urine testing, abdominal examination and pelvic floor tender-point examination are all core. The NIH-CPSI is the standard outcome tool.
s: Ch 56 Prostatitis, orchitis, epididymitis and scrotal pain

q: In UPOINT, what does 'N' stand for, and what does it imply?
o: Normal prostate
Neurologic/systemic: pain beyond the pelvis and overlapping conditions such as IBS, fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue, suggesting central sensitisation and a role for neuropathic pain drugs
Noninflammatory
Nonbacterial; antibiotics
e: UPOINT stands for Urinary, Psychosocial, Organ-specific, Infection, Neurologic/systemic, Tenderness. Treat all positive domains at the same time.
s: Ch 56 Prostatitis, orchitis, epididymitis and scrotal pain

q: Which statement about CPPS treatment is FALSE?
o: Repeated antibiotic courses are appropriate even without a positive culture
In meta-analyses the best combination was antibiotics plus α-blockers
Refer men with pelvic floor tenderness or high tone (such as obturator internus) for pelvic floor physical therapy and myofascial release
Sacral neuromodulation is an option when pain comes with frequency and urgency; men with bladder pain should get bladder-directed therapy
e: Do not give repeated antibiotics without a positive culture.
s: Ch 56 Prostatitis, orchitis, epididymitis and scrotal pain

q: Which statement is correct?
o: Antisperm granulomas define it
Autoimmune orchitis causes microlithiasis
Viral orchitis is mostly due to coxsackie virus
Mumps is the commonest viral cause; autoimmune orchitis is defined by antisperm antibodies (primary, relevant to infertility; secondary to vasculitis such as Behçet disease, PAN or HSP)
e: For acute scrotal pain or orchitis, Doppler ultrasound excludes torsion, mass or an anatomical abnormality. Mumps orchitis usually follows parotitis and can cause atrophy and subfertility.
s: Ch 56 Prostatitis, orchitis, epididymitis and scrotal pain

q: A 25-year-old with acute epididymitis denies sexual activity. The most likely cause is:
o: Brucella
E. coli
Chlamydia, so test regardless of the stated sexual history
Pseudomonas
e: Under 35, STIs (mainly chlamydia) are the main cause. Over 35, enteric organisms are.
s: Ch 56 Prostatitis, orchitis, epididymitis and scrotal pain

q: For chronic orchialgia with obturator internus tenderness, which is correct?
o: Go straight to denervation
Orchidectomy first
Opioids
Start with pelvic floor physical therapy and other conservative measures; Doppler ultrasound first to exclude anatomical causes, torsion or mass
e: Try all conservative measures before surgery.
s: Ch 56 Prostatitis, orchitis, epididymitis and scrotal pain

q: Which surgical detail is correct?
o: Ligate the lymphatics

The 'trifecta' targets are cremasteric fibres, the perivasal sheath and posterior lipomatous tissue; epididymectomy for post-vasectomy pain should include the distal vasectomy site; orchidectomy works better through an inguinal approach
Use a scrotal approach for orchidectomy
Microsurgical cord denervation targets the testicular artery and rete testis
e: Parekattil's group found the most Wallerian degeneration of nerves in these three areas.
s: Ch 56 Prostatitis, orchitis, epididymitis and scrotal pain

q: Which statement about defining IC/BPS is FALSE?
o: Urgency, glomerulations and hydrodistention findings are not needed for diagnosis
Pain, pressure or discomfort perceived to be related to the bladder is essential
Symptoms must last more than 6 weeks, without infection or other identifiable cause; it is a diagnosis of exclusion
The NIDDK criteria are the clinical definition and are highly sensitive
e: The NIDDK criteria were designed for research. They are specific but insensitive: 90% of experts agreed those meeting them had IC, but 60% of patients the experts diagnosed did not meet them. Pain usually builds as the bladder fills and drives the frequency. Symptom and problem indices (O'Leary–Sant) monitor severity and response, but do not diagnose.
s: Ch 57 Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome

q: Which statement about IC/BPS epidemiology is FALSE?
o: About 3 million women and 2 million men in the US have symptoms; clinical female-to-male ratio about 5:1
Average age of onset is about 40; childhood onset is extremely rare
Prevalence has fallen over time because of stricter definitions
Adult female first-degree relatives have about 17 times the prevalence
e: Prevalence has risen, probably because definitions became broader. Prodromal pelvic pain or voiding symptoms often go back decades before diagnosis, so presentation is usually subacute, often first treated as OAB or cystitis. Emotional, sexual or physical abuse is a risk factor (37% vs 22% of controls). Sexual dysfunction greatly affects quality of life.
s: Ch 57 Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome

q: Which condition is NOT over-represented in IC/BPS?
o: Irritable bowel syndrome
Chronic fatigue and atopic allergy
Fibromyalgia
Diabetes
e: MAPP found two pain phenotypes: pelvic pain only, and 'pelvic pain and beyond' (over 75%), pointing to central nervous system pain. High-tone pelvic floor dysfunction is present in 70–94%. Other overlapping problems include OAB, vulvodynia and IBS, so a multidisciplinary approach is needed. Missing these other pain generators is a common reason for poor results.
s: Ch 57 Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome

q: Which statement about Hunner lesions is FALSE?
o: Microscopic haematuria reliably predicts a Hunner lesion
They are the pathognomonic finding of 'classic' IC, found in a minority, and seen on office cystoscopy (distension or narrow-band imaging can help)
Histology shows a dense, often full-thickness lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate; biopsy them to exclude CIS
Patients with them tend to be older, have fewer comorbidities, and respond to fulguration or steroid injection: the only phenotype with a distinct treatment response and natural history
e: Haematuria and pyuria do not predict a Hunner lesion. Do cystoscopy if one is suspected or empirical treatment fails. Clinical presentation does not reliably differ with or without lesions. Lesions are always above the trigone, so a trigonal lesion suggests CIS. A Hunner lesion is not the same as a glomerulation, and it is not diagnostic without symptoms.
s: Ch 57 Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome

q: Which statement about IC/BPS pathophysiology is FALSE?
o: Antiproliferative factor (APF) from urothelium inhibits urothelial growth and is the most sensitive and specific urinary marker
Active infection drives the disease, so long-term antibiotics are the treatment
Mast cells (near vessels, nerves and muscle) play a central, though not primary, role in non-Hunner disease
Proposed mechanisms: leaky epithelium, mast cell activation, neurogenic inflammation, cross-sensitisation between pelvic organs, plus global CNS pain processes
e: Antibiotics are not indicated. A single doxycycline trial is reasonable only if the patient has never had one.
s: Ch 57 Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome

q: A 27-year-old with IC-like symptoms has gross haematuria and severe bladder inflammation. What history is key?
o: Recreational drug use, particularly ketamine, which causes lower and upper tract inflammation
Mast cell count
HbA1c
Endometriosis laparoscopy
e: Also exclude bladder cancer and TB. Men with irritative symptoms and pelvic pain need assessment for bacterial cystitis, bacterial prostatitis, IC/BPS and CIS. Many have had unnecessary bladder neck surgery. Some men with category III CPPS also meet IC/BPS criteria. Bacterial prostatitis (types I and II) is unrelated to IC/BPS.
s: Ch 57 Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome

q: The relationship of IC/BPS to bladder cancer is best described as:
o: Dysplasia is typical
Premalignant
Strong association
Most reports show no association; apparent links reflect misdiagnosed cancer (a Taiwanese study reported RR 2.95), so never ignore positive cytology
e: In the Mayo series of the 1970s, 12 of 53 men treated for IC had bladder cancer, through misdiagnosis rather than progression.
s: Ch 57 Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome

q: Which statement about tests in IC/BPS is FALSE?
o: Histology's main role is excluding other disease; there is no diagnostic histology, and inflammation is seen in 24–76%
Glomerulations are specific for IC/BPS
The potassium chloride test is neither sensitive nor specific (up to 25% of NIDDK-positive patients test negative), is painful and does not guide treatment
Urodynamics: reduced capacity and hypersensitivity with normal compliance; detrusor overactivity in about 15% is incidental
e: Glomerulations also occur after radiation, with cancer, after toxins or chemotherapy, on dialysis, and after diversion. They mean nothing in a patient without symptoms. The KCl test is positive in radiation cystitis, UTI, prostatitis and women with pelvic pain.
s: Ch 57 Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome

q: Which statement about hydrodistention under anaesthesia is correct?
o: Its main use is finding Hunner lesions; 30–50% get short-term relief and about 30% a brief flare; an anaesthetic capacity under 200 mL predicts a poor outcome and a more bladder-focused phenotype
It is required for diagnosis
It is diagnostic when glomerulations appear
It worsens all patients
e: A low anaesthetic capacity goes with higher symptom scores and less depression and IBS.
s: Ch 57 Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome

q: Which statement on initial management is FALSE?
o: Flares last days, typically triggered by diet and physical activity including sex
First-line also includes dietary changes (elimination diet), simple analgesics, pelvic floor relaxation and stress management
Start with the most aggressive therapy in all patients
Patient education is the most important first step: the condition is chronic, waxes and wanes, and remits often
e: Move to more aggressive care only if symptoms stay poorly controlled. Escalate early only if severe symptoms are unlikely to respond to conservative care. Patients who are poorly informed and desperate are vulnerable to exploitation.
s: Ch 57 Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome

q: Which statement about oral IC/BPS drugs is FALSE?
o: Amitriptyline helps sleep and neuropathic pain, and has antihistamine and anticholinergic effects, at doses below antidepressant levels
Amitriptyline is FDA-approved for IC/BPS
Amitriptyline's anticholinergic effect can worsen constipation and obstructive voiding
Pentosan polysulfate (an oral heparin analogue targeting the GAG layer) is one of two FDA-approved agents, but long-term use can cause pigmentary maculopathy
e: Amitriptyline is not FDA-approved but remains a mainstay. Its benefit in IC/BPS is not from its antidepressant effect. The two FDA-approved treatments are oral pentosan polysulfate and intravesical DMSO.
s: Ch 57 Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome

q: Which statement is correct?
o: Maintenance schedules are well established

No intravesical agent (BCG, lidocaine, Botox, heparin) has proven efficacy in pivotal double-blind trials, apart from the long-approved DMSO; intravesical therapy helps least where other pain generators dominate, such as vestibulodynia or high-tone pelvic floor dysfunction
Intravesical therapy is best for centralised pain
Intravesical BCG has proven efficacy
e: How often to give intravesical therapy, for how long, and whether maintenance helps have not been well studied.
s: Ch 57 Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome

q: Which statement about later-line therapy is FALSE?
o: Opioids have no dose ceiling, cause constipation and sedation, and long-term use produces physical dependence; they can be used for severe disease with 'universal precautions'
Be cautious with Botox when there are obstructive voiding symptoms or high-tone pelvic floor dysfunction (retention risk)
Opioids always cause addiction and must never be used
Sacral neuromodulation and intradetrusor Botox are fourth-line in the chapter's AUA algorithm
e: The 2022 AUA amendment dropped the strict tiers in favour of shared decision-making, but Botox and neuromodulation still come after first-line measures.
s: Ch 57 Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome (updated)

q: Which statement about surgery for IC/BPS is FALSE?
o: Before supratrigonal cystectomy with augmentation, urethral pain is the key concern, because up to 30% need self-catheterisation
The best surgical candidates have a clear bladder source (such as Hunner lesions) with a small, poorly compliant bladder
Sympathectomy, cystolysis and phenol injection of the pelvic plexus are reasonable options
Transurethral fulguration or steroid injection of Hunner lesions can relieve symptoms
e: Those operations have no role. Even cystectomy with diversion cannot guarantee freedom from pain. Cystoplasty or diversion can fail because the bowel segment becomes painful or contracts. Extravesical fat stranding on CT reflects full-thickness inflammation and does not affect the decision.
s: Ch 57 Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome

q: A woman with IC/BPS has deep dyspareunia, constipation-predominant IBS, hesitancy and straining to void. Which therapy is LEAST likely to help?
o: Pelvic floor physical therapy
Behavioural modification
Neuromodulation
Bladder chemodenervation (Botox)
e: She probably has high-tone pelvic floor dysfunction with obstructive symptoms. Muscle relaxants and physical therapy suit her. Botox risks retention.
s: Ch 57 Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome
